title: An archive is a second runway
governingQuestion: Who can retrieve New York fashion after the invitation, stream and venue disappear?
rightsBoundary: Protected invitations, films, backstage photography and organizer interfaces remain authorized-embed, link-only, or permission candidates. No reproduction right is inferred from public access.

beats.direction: Use the recurring witness with an on-screen disclaimer: CITY CONTEXT / NOT DAY-SPECIFIC.
beats.voice: New York makes time itself operational: calendar authority, dispersed venues, capture, broadcast, production labor, orders and memory must coordinate. This chapter follows memory: The venue disappears, schedules change and links decay; preservation choices determine which technical history remains citable and contestable.
beats.onScreen: Then: A 1982 Library of Congress photograph of Liz Claiborne with a model survives as an item-level, citable New York fashion record.

beats.direction: Animate only line reveals and state changes in the original evidence diagram.
beats.voice: A 1982 Library of Congress photograph of Liz Claiborne with a model survives as an item-level, citable New York fashion record. That earlier record fixes a point in time; it does not prove an inevitable progression toward the present.
beats.onScreen: Now: The NYPL preserves Patrick Kelly audiovisual recordings, while The Met describes onsite research access to major runway-photography and runway-video databases.
beats.credit: Graphic © Rayven-Nikkita Collins; sources in claim ledger

beats.direction: Animate only line reveals and state changes in the original evidence diagram.
beats.voice: The distinction is material. A polished interface can survive after its workers, contracts, specifications or permission trail disappear, leaving the audience with an outcome but not its operating history.
beats.onScreen: Next: No public record reviewed establishes a complete, rights-cleared archive of every official NYFW show, worker, venue, invitation and technical credit.
